title: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME): The Master Clinician's Guide
summary: DME is the leading cause of vision loss in the working-age population. This comprehensive guide covers the intricate pathophysiology, evolving classification systems, and the evidence-based management protocols established by landmark clinical trials.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is defined as the accumulation of fluid in the intraretinal layers (outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers) and/or subretinal space within the macular region. It results from a breakdown of the inner and outer blood-retinal barriers (BRB), primarily triggered by chronic hyperglycemia-induced microvascular damage. It can occur at any stage of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR).

sections.title: ETDRS Criteria: Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME)

rows: Thickening at or within 500 µm of the center of the fovea.
HE at or within 500 µm with adjacent retinal thickening.
Retinal thickening ≥ 1 disc area in size, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the foveal center.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Painless, gradual blurriness of central vision.
Metamorphopsia (distorted lines).
Micropsia / Macropsia.
Reduced contrast sensitivity.
Central or paracentral scotoma.
Hard exudates in a circinate pattern.
Microaneurysms (MA) and dot-blot hemorrhages.

rows: Post-cataract surgery; classic petaloid leakage on FFA.
Right-angle vessels; temporal foveal atrophy; no lipid.
History of head/neck radiation; sluggish capillary refill.

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management (DRCR.net Protocols)
content: Step 1: Systemic Optimization (HbA1c < 7.0%, Blood Pressure < 130/80, Lipids).
Step 2: Center-Involved (CI-DME) with VA 20/25 or better: Observation (Protocol V).
Step 3: CI-DME with VA 20/30 or worse: First-line Anti-VEGF (Protocol T).
Step 4: Non-Center Involved DME: Focal/Grid Laser (ETDRS Guidelines).
Step 5: Refractory to Anti-VEGF: Switch agents or add Intravitreal Steroids (Ozurdex/Iluvien).
Step 6: VMT-associated DME: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).

rows: VEGF-Trap; superior in VA < 20/50 baseline (Protocol T).
Fab fragment; highly effective in all VA ranges.
Non-erodible implant; lasts up to 36 months.

sections.title: Red Flags: Steroid Precautions
content: Pre-existing Glaucoma (High risk of IOP spike).
Advanced Cup-to-Disc ratio (> 0.8).
Phakic Status (Steroids accelerate cataract formation).
History of Herpetic Keratitis/Endophthalmitis.
Active Ocular Infection.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials Summary
content: ETDRS: Focal/Grid laser reduces risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Protocol T: Aflibercept performed better than Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab in patients with VA 20/50 or worse at 1 year.
Protocol I: Anti-VEGF + prompt or deferred laser is superior to laser alone.
Protocol V: Patients with 20/25 vision can be observed safely if monitored closely.
PANORAMA: Aflibercept can improve DR severity scales and prevent DME.
YOSEMITE/RHINE: Faricimab (Ang-2/VEGF) shows non-inferiority with potential for Q16 dosing.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV for DME
content: 1. Core Vitrectomy with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) induction.
2. Removal of the Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) using ICG or Brilliant Blue G.
3. Release of any tangential traction or epiretinal membranes.
4. Consideration of steroid injection or endolaser if needed.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: DRIL (Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers) is a strong biomarker for poor visual prognosis.
Hard exudates in the fovea can lead to permanent photoreceptor loss and subfoveal fibrosis.
Anemia and Renal Disease (high Creatinine) are strong systemic drivers of DME severity.
In pregnancy, DME may worsen significantly but often regresses postpartum.
